Learnit App

Role: Product Designer  ·  Tools: Figma, Firebase, Google Analytics

My Role: In this case study, I have been researching Learnit, which is a learning English application.

Duration: May 2023 – Aug 2023

Table of contents
The objective The Impact Background Research Plan & Research The problem(s) or Question(s) Ideation Visual design Prototype & Test Conclusion
The objective

The main goal of this project was to improve user retention and engagement in the Learnit app. Analytics showed that retention rates and engagement were close to 0%, while nearly 500 new users joined daily. I aimed to redesign key flows, enhance feature discoverability, and create a more engaging learning experience.

Stakeholders

Most users tickets                            Firebase

The Impact
  • Increased user retention by designing flows that encourage regular practice.
  • Boosted engagement through gamification and social interaction features.
  • Provided variety and fresh content to keep users motivated.
  • Improved progress tracking and personalized feedback for better learning outcomes.
Background

Learnit is a language learning application with multiple features. Initially, the app lacked AI integration, proper content organization, and engaging experiences, resulting in low retention. My role was to research, ideate, and design better user flows to increase engagement and user satisfaction.

Research Plan & Research

Current IA

Methods Used:

  • Analytics (Firebase)
  • User task testing
  • User interviews and tickets analysis

Key Findings:

  1. Important pages, like grammar summaries, were missing or hard to find.
  2. Unrelated content was often grouped in the same section.
  3. Active users were fewer than new users, and competitive/entertainment features were unclear.
  4. Many features were built without user research and remained untested.
  5. Return rate and engagement were extremely low despite a high influx of new users.

Insights:

  • Retention Challenge
  • Sustained Engagement
  • Variety and Fresh Content
The problem(s) or Question(s)

Card sorting

  • User Drop-off: Users often discontinue after initial stages due to lack of motivation or habit formation.
  • Declining Engagement: Initial excitement fades, and users struggle to stay motivated.
  • Monotony: Limited variety and fresh content reduces interest.
  • Limited Social Interaction: Lack of community features hinders motivation and collaborative learning.
  • Insufficient Feedback: Users cannot easily track progress or receive meaningful feedback.
Ideation

Brainstorming:

  • Mind mapping and sketching to explore multiple solutions.
  • Focused on gamification, social features, and better content discovery.

Concept Development:

  • Created user flows and low-fidelity wireframes to refine ideas.
  • Developed home page and leaderboard concepts to improve onboarding and engagement.

Selection:

  • Prioritized features based on feasibility, user needs, and business goals.
  • Decided to focus on progress tracking, sorting cards for better navigation, and gamified interactions.

User flow & Prototype

Prototype & Test

Prototype Creation: Created high-fidelity prototype in Figma for testing new flows and interactions.

Interactions: Key interactions included content sorting, progress tracking, gamified rewards, and social features.

Feedback & Iterations:

  • User testing revealed confusion in navigation.
  • Iterated the design for clarity and improved usability.
  • Implemented final solutions based on feedback and research insights.
Conclusion

By applying research-driven design, ideation, and iterative prototyping, the Learnit app was transformed into a more engaging, motivating, and user-friendly platform. Users were able to better track their progress, enjoy varied content, interact socially, and remain engaged throughout their learning journey.

My Role: Product Designer

Status: Released

Case Study Summary

This case study focuses on redesigning the Dealer App to improve clarity, transparency, and control for professional dealers by simplifying complex flows such as auctions, orders, and payments.

The result was higher user efficiency and trust, reduced support dependency, and improved engagement and retention while preserving critical business data integrity.

Table of contents
The objective The Impact Background Research Plan & Research The problem(s) or Question(s) Ideation Visual design Prototype & Test Conclusion
The objective

The Dealer App was created for active buyers in the automotive market — users who interact with multiple listings, conversations, and decisions on a daily basis. Before this project, the experience felt fragmented. Users often got lost in the flow, struggled to keep track of their personal history, and had limited control over their own settings.

This project aimed to reshape that experience into something more professional, clear, and dependable. On the business side, the goal was to reduce reliance on support, while increasing conversion, engagement, and long-term retention.

The Impact
  1. Improved User Efficiency & Reduced Confusion — Dealers could navigate auctions, orders, and payments more quickly thanks to real-time status indicators and clear stepwise updates.
  2. Increased Transparency & Trust — Contextual feedback for cancellations and structured vehicle inspection information made users feel more confident.
  3. Enhanced Financial & Operational Accuracy — Stepwise payment visibility, proper wallet integration, and settlement tracking ensured transparent transactions.
  4. Higher Engagement & Retention — Clear processes, actionable notifications, and visible outcomes encouraged users to stay active.
  5. Business Alignment — Maintaining data integrity while improving UX protected business-critical information and reduced support workload.
Background

This project began in response to a combination of business requests, user complaints, and data analysis focused on critical user flows. Although the Dealer App already existed, insights showed that several high-impact journeys — particularly around auctions and order management — were creating friction and negatively affecting user satisfaction.

From a business perspective, the accuracy and reliability of data were highly critical, which introduced constraints and influenced many design decisions. Project success was primarily measured by improved user satisfaction while maintaining the integrity of essential business data.

Research Plan & Research

A mixed-method research approach was conducted, including usability testing, user interviews with active dealers, support team interviews, and detailed review of behavioral and business data.

Key Insights:

  1. Lack of transparency was the core issue — users felt uncertain about auction, order, payment, and legal document statuses.
  2. Transaction history and order tracking were especially critical — users needed precise timestamps and reliable records.
  3. The auction experience itself was a major source of friction — users struggled to distinguish winning, losing, and canceled auctions.
  4. Financial and legal processes created additional complexity with multi-step payment methods and unclear document requirements.
  5. Search and filtering were insufficient across auctions, deposits, orders, and history.
  6. Users needed timely, actionable notifications — missing or unclear alerts caused constant app-checking or support calls.
The problem(s) or Question(s)
  1. Time loss and cognitive overload — Dealers spent excessive time navigating complex, fragmented flows with unclear statuses and long wait times.
  2. Lack of clear order and transaction tracking — Users had limited visibility into real-time status of orders, payments, documents, and legal processes.
  3. Lack of transparency without compromising business data — Dealers needed clear information while sensitive business data couldn't be fully exposed.

HMW

"How might we provide dealers with clear, timely, and trustworthy information that reduces confusion and saves time, while ensuring business-critical data remains protected and reliable?"

Ideation
  • Clear Status Communication — Show current step of orders, auctions, and payments with estimated timelines.
  • Transparent Cancellation & Outcome Reasons — Always display why an auction or order was canceled.
  • Payment & Settlement Visibility — Clear information about payment status, pending settlements, and expected completion time.
  • Vehicle & Inspection Transparency — Show engine, chassis, and body status with defect intensity levels.
  • Actionable Notifications — Notify users about every critical step in real time.
  • Balance Between Transparency and Business Safety — Provide all user-relevant information while keeping sensitive data hidden.

Principle: "Transparency is not exposing all internal data. It is clearly communicating what is happening, why it matters to the user, and what comes next."

Prototype & Test
  1. Usability Testing — Conducted on previous version and prototypes to identify friction in auctions, orders, payments, and legal processes.
  2. Clarity & Comprehension Testing — Tested whether users could understand status updates, cancellation reasons, and notifications.
  3. User Interviews — Conducted with professional dealers and support staff to gather qualitative insights.
  4. Data-Driven Analysis — Analyzed behavioral and transaction data to identify bottlenecks and abandoned flows.
  5. Feedback Iteration — Continuously refined designs based on testing results.
  6. Stakeholder Reviews — Presented prototypes to product, analytics, and support teams to ensure alignment.
Conclusion

The Dealer App redesign focused on addressing core challenges: time loss, confusion, unclear order and auction statuses, and lack of transparent but secure information. Design decisions prioritized clarity, transparency, and actionable feedback, while safeguarding sensitive business data.

↑ User efficiency & trust ↓ Support dependency ↑ Engagement & retention ✓ Business data integrity

Order Journey (Dealer)

Role: Senior Product Designer  ·  Tools: Figma, Clarity, Firebase, Google Analytics
Skills & Methods
Accessibility Interview Prototyping Usability testing Userflow
Tools
Clarity Figma Firebase Google Analytics

My Role: As a Senior Product Designer, I led the design of a transparent Order Management system for dealers, simplifying the process and improving usability. I collaborated with cross-functional teams, conducted user research, and created a clear status and notification system.

Team: Other designers, Research, Analytics, Developers, Product Manager, Operations, Logistics

Duration: Dec 2024 – July 2025  ·  Status: Released

Portfolio Summary

This project focused on redesigning the Dealer Order Management journey to make complex processes clear and transparent for dealers. The result was reduced support dependency, faster order completion, and a more efficient, trustworthy experience across orders, payments, and documents.

Table of contents
The objective The Problem The Job To Be Done Solution Strategy & Design Decisions The Process of Redesign Outcome and Impact Visual design Conclusion
The objective

What was the problem? The Order Management system at Khodro45 was too complex. Dealers couldn't easily track the status of vehicles and orders. They didn't know the current state of their transactions, and had to contact support to clarify.

What was the goal? To create a transparent, easy-to-understand system for dealers, allowing them to track orders, document statuses, and payment statuses without confusion.

Why was it important? The complexity led to increased support calls, frustration, and lower conversion rates.

The Problem

Current version                                          Current Flow version

  • Why did the problem exist? Multiple disconnected processes (Auction, Order, Payment, Document) without a unified tracking system. The internal status system was shown directly to dealers, making it hard to understand their current order status.
  • What made it significant? Dealers didn't know what the current step was, whether they needed to take action or wait, or what the next step would be.
The Job To Be Done (JTBD)

Who was experiencing the problem? Primary users were dealers going through the purchasing and order process. Secondary users were operations, legal, and finance teams.

  • Dealers needed to know where they stood in the process.
  • They needed clear guidance on what action (if any) they had to take next.
  • They needed to track the status of documents and payments with transparency.

"The dealer needs to know where their order is, what action they need to take, and when they should expect the next steps."

Solution Strategy & Design Decisions
  • Status Mapping & Categorisation — Identified and categorised all statuses into three groups: Negotiation, Contract, and Ownership Transfer. Separated internal statuses from user-facing ones.
  • Order Flow Redesign — Designed a single dashboard where dealers could track orders from auction to delivery. Dealers only saw actionable and relevant statuses.
  • Notification System — Automatic notifications for each status change, divided into Actionable (dealer needs to act) and Informational (status update).
  • Payment & Legal Process Simplification — Simplified how dealers track payments, document submission, and legal review.
The Process of Redesign
  1. Initial Research & Problem Definition — Analyzed dealer pain points through interviews and support data.
  2. Categorization & Simplification — Grouped statuses based on the journey: Negotiation, Contract, Ownership Transfer.
  3. Collaborative Work with Operations & Legal — Ensured design decisions aligned with operational needs.
  4. Designing the Dashboard & Notification System — Built and iterated on the core tracking experience.
Outcome and Impact
  1. Clear and Transparent Process — Dealers could now track their orders with clarity.
  2. Reduction in Support Calls — With clear visibility, dealers no longer needed to call support for every update.
  3. Improved Conversion Rates — Dealers acted more efficiently, moving through the order process faster.
  4. Effective Notifications — Dealers were informed automatically about every step.

V1 — we tested with over 50 users across many versions

Usability outcome

Usability outcome & Changing

Visual design

Final versions

Conclusion

The redesign resulted in a clear, efficient, and easy-to-understand system that helped dealers track their orders, payments, and documents. This ultimately reduced support calls, improved conversion rates, and enhanced the dealer experience.

↓ Support calls ↑ Conversion rate ↑ Dealer efficiency ↑ Trust in system Faster order completion
Featured · B2B Automotive · Khodro45

Khodro45 Dealer

Role: Senior Product Designer · Status: Multiple releases · Team: Product, engineering, research, operations
My contribution: Led and contributed to product design across dealer-facing flows — from discovery and IA through prototyping, usability testing, and design system alignment. Worked cross-functionally with PM, engineering, research, analytics, and operations.
Context

Khodro45 operates in the automotive market with professional dealers as primary users. The dealer product spans high-stakes workflows: auctions, order management, payments, legal checks, documents, and operational dashboards — all requiring accuracy, transparency, and speed.

Problem

Dealers faced fragmented, opaque flows. Critical statuses (auctions, orders, payments, documents) were hard to track. This increased support load, slowed decisions, and reduced trust — especially where business data sensitivity limited what could be exposed.

Users
  • Primary: professional automotive dealers managing daily auctions, orders, and transactions
  • Secondary: operations, legal, finance, and support teams
Research

Mixed methods: usability testing with dealers (conducted regularly across iterations), user interviews, support team input, and behavioral/product data review.

Insights
  • Transparency — not exposing all internal data, but clearly communicating status, next steps, and reasons
  • Order and transaction tracking are critical trust surfaces
  • Auction outcomes, payments, and legal steps create the most friction when unclear
  • Search, filtering, and notifications must be actionable, not decorative
Design challenges
  • Balancing operational transparency with business data sensitivity
  • Multiple parallel workflows (auctions, orders, payments, legal) with different mental models
  • Legacy complexity vs. need for a scalable design system
  • High-stakes decisions requiring clarity under time pressure
Exploration

Explored navigation models, status communication patterns, notification hierarchies, and dashboard information architecture — prototyping alternatives before converging on stepwise visibility and actionable notifications.

Design scope

Work across the dealer ecosystem, grouped by product problem:

Order & transaction flows
Order Journey Wizard redesign Payment integration Car Document Delivery
Dealer operations
Dealer Dashboard Activity Dashboard Dealer History Auction Hall
Trust & engagement
Rate & Review Affiliate Flow Ticketing System Legal Check AI
Foundation
Dealer App Design System
Decisions

Prioritized dealer-facing clarity over internal completeness. Chose progressive disclosure for complex flows. Aligned design system tokens early so engineering could ship consistently across parallel workstreams.

Solution
  • Separated internal vs. user-facing statuses for clearer dealer communication
  • Stepwise visibility for orders, payments, and documents
  • Actionable vs. informational notification model
  • Design system components to accelerate consistent delivery across flows

For deep dives: Dealer App redesign · Order Journey

Iteration

Designs were tested with dealers throughout — usability sessions informed navigation clarity, status communication, and notification comprehension before release.

Learnings

In B2B products with sensitive data, clarity is a design constraint — not a nice-to-have. The best outcomes came from aligning operational reality with what dealers actually need to act, not from showing everything at once.

TapsiFood

Role: Senior Product Designer · Apr – Nov 2024 · Team: Product, engineering, UX research
My contribution: Product design for vendor and commerce-related flows — from IA and flow design through prototyping and cross-functional iteration with research and engineering.
Context

TapsiFood operates in food delivery with restaurant partners managing orders, menus, and daily operations through vendor-facing products. The experience needed to support operational complexity without overwhelming partners.

Problem

Vendor workflows involved multiple steps, statuses, and operational tasks. The product needed clearer structure, better usability across key journeys, and alignment between business requirements and partner mental models.

Users
  • Primary: restaurant partners managing orders, menus, and daily operations
  • Secondary: product, engineering, and operations teams supporting the vendor platform
Research

Collaborated with UX research and cross-functional partners on system-level decisions — mapping real vendor tasks, reviewing existing flows, and iterating based on partner needs and product constraints.

Insights
  • High-frequency tasks need clarity and scannability — not more screens
  • Vendor mental models differ from consumer food delivery experiences
  • Operational complexity must be structured, not hidden
  • System-level IA decisions affect every downstream flow
Design challenges
  • Balancing business requirements with partner usability
  • Redesigning vendor and commerce flows without disrupting live operations
  • Multiple parallel workflows with different urgency and frequency
  • Aligning design decisions across product, research, and engineering
Exploration

Explored information architecture, vendor journey maps, and flow alternatives for e-commerce and platform experiences — prototyping and iterating with research and engineering before converging on clearer structure and reduced friction.

Design scope

Work across the vendor ecosystem, grouped by product problem:

Vendor operations
Order management Menu management Daily operations
Commerce & platform
E-commerce flows Vendor platform redesign
Foundation
Information architecture Flow design Prototyping
Decisions

Prioritized product thinking before UI execution. Focused on system-level structure so individual flows could scale consistently. Partnered with research and engineering early on IA and flow decisions.

Solution
  • Clearer vendor platform structure for high-frequency operational tasks
  • Redesigned e-commerce and vendor flows with improved scannability
  • Cross-functional alignment on system-level design decisions
  • Iterative prototyping to validate flow clarity before implementation
Iteration

Designs were iterated with UX research and engineering throughout — flow structure, task clarity, and platform usability informed each round of refinement.

Learnings

In high-frequency marketplace products, clarity in everyday tasks matters as much as flagship features. The best vendor experiences reduce cognitive load in the flows partners use most often.

Featured · Automotive market data · Sanjeh

Sanjeh

Role: Product Designer · Area: Automotive market intelligence
My contribution: Product thinking around how complex automotive market data becomes understandable — valuation, trends, comparisons, and transaction transparency.
Context

Sanjeh sits in the automotive market data space, where users need to understand value, pricing, and market movement — often across dense, technical information.

Problem

Market data is inherently complex: used and new car prices, valuation models, trend lines, and comparisons with other assets (gold, dollar, stocks, Bitcoin). Users need clarity without losing nuance or trust.

Users
  • Primary: car owners and buyers seeking valuation, pricing, and market context
  • Secondary: users comparing automotive value against other assets and market trends
Research

Product thinking focused on how people interpret market data — what they need to act on vs. what creates noise. Structured around real questions: what is my car worth, how is the market moving, and how does it compare.

Insights
  • Complex data needs hierarchy — not more density on one screen
  • Valuation and ownership context are different mental models than market trends
  • Cross-asset comparisons require careful framing to stay trustworthy
  • Real transaction data only helps when it becomes understandable, not just visible
Design challenges
  • Turning dense market information into scannable, actionable experiences
  • Balancing expert-level data with everyday user comprehension
  • Presenting trends and comparisons without oversimplifying nuance
  • Building trust when data sources and models are inherently complex
Exploration

Explored information hierarchy, progressive disclosure, and data presentation patterns — how to surface valuation, trends, and comparisons in ways that respect both the complexity of the data and the clarity users need.

Design scope

Work across the product, grouped by user need:

Ownership & valuation
Value of my cars Car valuation Used car price estimation
Market intelligence
New car prices Market analysis Market trends
Context & comparison
Gold, dollar, stocks, Bitcoin Real transaction data
Decisions

Prioritized understandable experiences over data completeness. Used structured hierarchy and progressive disclosure so users could go deeper when needed — without facing everything at once.

Solution
  • Clear information hierarchy for valuation, pricing, and market movement
  • Separated ownership context from broader market trends
  • Framed cross-asset comparisons in language users can act on
  • Made real transaction data accessible through structure, not just display
Iteration

Design directions were refined around how users interpret market data — testing whether hierarchy, labeling, and disclosure patterns made complex information feel clearer and more trustworthy.

Learnings

In data-heavy products, the design problem is rarely the data itself — it's how people make sense of it. Turning complex market information into understandable experiences is a product design challenge, not just a visualization one.
